\large Predicting Model Merging Success from Weight- and Representation-Space Signals}

\begin{center}\today\end{center}

\begin{dlaiauthorlist}

\begin{abstract}
Model merging combines models fine-tuned from a common checkpoint by arithmetic on their weights, but whether a merge works is usually discovered only after performing it. We ask whether the pre-merge signal that best predicts merging damage depends on the merging algorithm. We fine-tune \nFTall{} models on CIFAR-100 task families whose similarity is set by a five-level dial, run \nMergeAll{} merges with weight averaging, task arithmetic, TIES and DARE, and test five signals against trivial baselines. The answer is no: the same similarity signals predict the damage for all four algorithms. CKA is the most reliable diagnostic and the only one that keeps its sign on a ResNet-18 control, where weight-space cosine reverses. We also show that weighted sign conflict is a function of cosine, and that DARE's apparent failure is an untuned scaling.
\end{abstract}

% ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}

Fine-tuning a pretrained model $\theta_0$ on task $i$ gives $\theta_i = \theta_0 + \tau_i$, where the \emph{task vector} $\tau_i$ records what the task changed. Model merging builds one multi-task model by combining task vectors directly, with no data and no training~\cite{wortsman2022soups,ilharco2023editing}. It often works but fails silently: one finds out only by evaluating the merged model. Since merging algorithms work in different ways, they may fail for different reasons, which raises our question: \emph{does the signal that predicts merging damage depend on the algorithm?} If yes, the diagnostic must match the merger; if one signal dominates everywhere, mergeability is a property of the models and one diagnostic suffices; if nothing beats trivial baselines, the diagnostics themselves are in doubt. We wrote down in advance which signal we expected to matter for each algorithm (Table~\ref{tab:prereg}), built task families whose similarity we control by design, and tested the signals against baselines, with a stability control across seeds and architectures. Code and results: \url{https://github.com/vulpiani1948744-lab/dlai-mergeability}.

% ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Related work}\label{sec:related}

Model soups average fine-tuned weights~\cite{wortsman2022soups}; task arithmetic adds scaled task vectors~\cite{ilharco2023editing}; TIES trims small updates and resolves sign disagreements, which it identifies as a cause of interference~\cite{yadav2023ties}; DARE drops most delta parameters at random and rescales the rest~\cite{yu2024dare}. Linear CKA compares the representations of two networks~\cite{kornblith2019cka}. We turn these explanations of interference into predictors and test them across algorithms.

% ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Method}\label{sec:method}

\paragraph{A dial for task similarity.} CIFAR-100~\cite{krizhevsky2009cifar} is split into 5 tasks of 20 classes (10{,}000 training and 2{,}000 test images each). In the \emph{semantic} split each task joins four related superclasses (e.g.\ aquatic life, or outdoor scenes and vehicles), so the tasks need different features and merging should be hard; in the \emph{random} split every task is a miniature of the dataset and merging should be easy. A mixing fraction $\alpha \in \{0, .25, .5, .75, 1\}$ reassigns a random $\alpha$ share of the classes, keeping 20 classes per task; semantic purity falls \puritySemantic/\purityMixA/\purityMixB/\purityMixC/\purityRandom\%. Images, budget, hyperparameters and seeds (0, 1) are identical across levels.

\paragraph{Models and frozen heads.} We use ViT-Tiny~\cite{dosovitskiy2021vit} (ImageNet-pretrained, 5.5M parameters) at $128\times128$ (linear probe \resVitLow\% vs \resVitHigh\% at 224, for a third of the tokens). For each task we fit a logistic-regression head on frozen $\theta_0$ features and \emph{freeze} it before fine-tuning the encoder (5 epochs, AdamW, learning rate $10^{-4}$, cosine schedule): since every encoder is read out by heads matched to $\theta_0$, a post-merge drop measures merging damage, not a mismatched head. Fine-tuning gains \ftVitGainMin--\ftVitGainMax{} points over the probe. As a control we repeat this with ResNet-18~\cite{he2016resnet} on the two extreme levels, with BatchNorm statistics frozen and excluded from $\tau$ (left free, they corrupted the task vectors). This gives \nFTvit{} ViT and \nFTres{} ResNet task vectors, trained on the same GPU and checked for anomalous norms.

\paragraph{Merging algorithms.} The merged encoder is $\theta_0 + \tau_S$ for a subset $S$ of tasks. \emph{Averaging}: $\tau_S$ is the mean of the $\tau_i$. \emph{Task arithmetic}: $\tau_S = \lambda \sum_i \tau_i$, $\lambda \in \{.1, .2, .3, .5, 1\}$. \emph{TIES}: keep each $\tau_i$'s top 20\% entries, elect one sign per parameter, average the agreeing entries; $\lambda \in \{.5, 1\}$. \emph{DARE}: keep a random 10\% of each $\tau_i$, rescaled by 10, then TIES; $\lambda \in \{.2, .3, .5, 1\}$, the values below 1 added after a first run (Sec.~\ref{sec:results}). Averaging is task arithmetic with $\lambda = 1/|S|$.

\paragraph{Signals and baselines.} We test five signals, all computed before merging from the subset's task vectors (averaged over its pairs) and 2{,}000 unlabelled test images: the \emph{cosine} between task vectors; the \emph{sign conflict}, the share of $\sum_k |\tau_{a,k}\tau_{b,k}|$ on coordinates of opposite sign; the \emph{subspace overlap} of the top-8 singular directions of each layer's update; the \emph{CKA} between the features of two fine-tuned encoders; and the \emph{drift}, the CKA of each encoder with $\theta_0$ (high = little drift). A signal is useful only if it beats three trivial baselines: always predicting the mean (b0), the number of merged tasks (b1), and the task-vector norm $\lVert\tau\rVert$ (b2).

\paragraph{Outcome and statistics.} We merge all pairs, triples and the five-task set per level and seed (\nMergeVit{} ViT and \nMergeRes{} ResNet merges). The outcome is \emph{normalized accuracy}, the mean over merged tasks of merged over fine-tuned test accuracy, at each algorithm's best setting (a fixed setting changes no correlation by more than \fixedMaxDelta). Spearman $\rho$ is computed within pairs and within triples and averaged, which removes b1; partial $\rho$ given $\lVert\tau\rVert$ addresses b2. Stability is the Kendall $\tau$ between signal rankings; generalization is tested by ridge regression fitted on four similarity levels and tested on the fifth.

% ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Results}\label{sec:results}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig_dial.pdf}
\caption{ViT-Tiny. (a) Normalized accuracy against the mixing fraction (mean of the four algorithms at their best setting; bars: two seeds). (b) Five-task merges against $\lambda$.}
\label{fig:dial}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{The dial works.} Merging gets easier as tasks become alike (Fig.~\ref{fig:dial}a): five-task merges rise from \dialSemFive\% to \dialRandFive\%, pairs from \dialSemTwo\% to \dialRandTwo\%. No merge fails outright at its best setting (ViT minimum \tunedMinVit\%), so the signals must rank differences of a few points.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_signals.pdf}
\caption{Spearman $\rho$ of each signal with normalized accuracy, within subset size; boxes mark the pre-registered signals. $^\dagger$DARE at $\lambda = 1$ only.}
\label{fig:signals}
\end{figure*}

\paragraph{The same signals for every algorithm.} On ViT, cosine, sign conflict, subspace overlap and CKA predict all four algorithms alike, $|\rho| = \rhoVitFamMin$--$\rhoVitFamMax$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:signals}), with differences inside the bootstrap intervals (e.g.\ CKA with task arithmetic, $[\ciVitCkaLo, \ciVitCkaHi]$); drift predicts nothing ($|\rho| \le \rhoVitDriftAbsMax$). The ranking among the four is not reproducible across seeds (Kendall $\tau$ from \kendallSeedVitMin{} to \kendallSeedVitMax) because they are nearly collinear ($|\rho| \ge \corrVitFamMin$ between any two): which one wins for an algorithm is noise. On ResNet-18 the ranking is stable across seeds ($\tau = \kendallSeedResMin$--$\kendallSeedResMax$) and the same for every algorithm ($\tau \ge \kendallAlgResMin$).

\paragraph{Beyond the baselines.} The norm alone predicts damage ($\rho = \rhoVitNormMin$ to $\rhoVitNormMax$), but the similarity signals survive conditioning on it (partial $|\rho| = \partVitFamMin$--$\partVitFamMax$) and predict an unseen similarity level: subset size and norm reach $R^2 = \rTwoBTwoMin$--$\rTwoBTwoMax$, adding CKA $\rTwoCkaMin$--$\rTwoCkaMax$, the best single signal. Within one level, however, $|\rho|$ falls to \rhoVitWithinMin--\rhoVitWithinMax.

\paragraph{Across architectures.} On ResNet-18 cosine \emph{reverses} sign ($\rho = \rhoResCosMin$ to $\rhoResCosMax$) and vanishes given the norm (partial $\rho = \partResCosMin$ to $\partResCosMax$): there it only measures distance travelled. Drift, silent on ViT, is the strongest signal ($\rho = \rhoResDriftMin$--$\rhoResDriftMax$). CKA is the only signal positive and robust to the norm on both backbones (partial $\rho = \partVitCkaMin$--$\partVitCkaMax$ on ViT, $\partResCkaMin$--$\partResCkaMax$ on ResNet).

\paragraph{Two findings about the methods.} With $S_\pm$ the sums of $|\tau_{a,k}\tau_{b,k}|$ over coordinates of equal ($+$) and opposite ($-$) sign, sign conflict is $c = S_-/(S_+ + S_-)$ and
\[
\cos(\tau_a, \tau_b) = (1 - 2c)\,\cos(|\tau_a|, |\tau_b|),
\]
so the two signals agree in rank (\corrCosSignVit{} here): the predictions for TIES and task arithmetic cannot be separated. Second, with 90\% of the entries dropped DARE's surviving supports barely overlap, so TIES's disjoint mean turns into a \emph{sum}: DARE tracks task arithmetic at the same $\lambda$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:dial}b, within \dareTaGapMax{} points for $\lambda \le .5$), collapses at $\lambda = 1$ (\dareOneFive\% on five tasks) and reaches \dareBestFive\% at $\lambda = \dareBestScale$. Only two of our four mechanisms are truly distinct.


% ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Discussion and conclusions}\label{sec:discussion}

In this setting mergeability behaves as a property of the models, not of the algorithm: one family of similarity signals predicts the damage for every algorithm, and CKA -- the best predictor of an unseen similarity level and the only one consistent across a Transformer and a CNN -- is the diagnostic to use. Of the pre-registered predictions (Table~\ref{tab:prereg}) only the one for task arithmetic held, and not specifically. The absence of algorithm-relativity has two causes worth designing around: redundant signals, and algorithms that reduce to task arithmetic.

\paragraph{Limitations.} Merges never failed badly (at least \tunedMinVit\% on ViT and \tunedMinRes\% on ResNet at the best setting), and most predictive power separates similarity levels rather than subsets within one. Models are small, on one dataset at $128\times128$, with two seeds; subsets share tasks, so bootstrap intervals are optimistic. The ResNet control covers two levels with DARE at $\lambda = 1$ only, and hyperparameters were selected on the evaluation split. A heterogeneous benchmark, a layer-wise CKA ablation and effective rank were planned but not done. The DARE sweep was recomputed on another device from the same task vectors and matched the original run.
